heads.title: Cloud-provider capex expectations have reset higher, but remain forecasts
heads.thesis: Current research supports substantially higher 2026 hyperscaler capex expectations, with aggregate estimates near $800 billion and company guidance pointing to large outlays. The mechanism is continued AI-infrastructure investment; the limitation is that the aggregate is forecast, not confirmed full-year spending, and individual company guidance is not an actual result.

claims.text: Analyst consensus and a Goldman Sachs estimate place five hyperscalers’ 2026 capex or AI-infrastructure investment near $800 billion, above earlier estimates of roughly $733 billion for five companies and $745 billion for four.
Company-level guidance is consistent with high spending: Alphabet raised its 2026 capex range to $195–205 billion, while Amazon raised its cash capex expectation to about $220 billion.
For Meta, management’s FY2026 range is $130–145 billion, and Microsoft’s calendar-2026 expectation is about $175 billion; these are company forecasts, not realized annual totals.
TSMC’s planned 2026 capex remains $52–56 billion; rising packaging capex share is not evidence that the total plan has been raised.

limitations: The near-$800 billion aggregate is driven primarily by analyst and third-party forecasts; full-year 2026 actual spending is not yet established.
Company guidance and industry-wide totals have different scopes and should not be treated as interchangeable.
watch_questions: Do hyperscalers report actual 2026 capex that confirms the near-$800 billion aggregate?
Do company guidance ranges change, and do reported totals use consistent lease and cash-capex definitions?

heads.title: AI demand supports strong NVIDIA growth, while revenue conversion remains unproven
heads.thesis: Current evidence supports strong FY2027 NVIDIA revenue growth, especially in Data Center and Compute & Networking, through Blackwell deployment and AI-infrastructure demand. It does not yet establish the higher annual revenue thresholds under consideration: much of the forward support is forecast or customer spending intent, while infrastructure constraints, customer concentration, and China-market limits remain relevant.

claims.text: NVIDIA reported FY2026 revenue of $215.9 billion and FY2027 Q1 revenue of $81.6 billion; the $91 billion Q2 figure is guidance, not realized revenue. Third-party FY2027 growth forecasts of 80–82% support a strong full-year outlook but remain forecasts.

FY2027 Q1 Data Center revenue was $75.2 billion, up 92% year over year, with growth attributed to Blackwell 300 ramp and networking demand; this supports continued growth but does not establish the full-year segment result.
Compute & Networking generated $74.55 billion in FY2027 Q1, up 88% year over year. Simple annualization approaches the $300 billion threshold, but one quarter does not confirm a full-year result.
Customer concentration and infrastructure availability are risks to converting demand into revenue; NVIDIA also reported it was effectively foreclosed from China’s data-center compute market.
Hyperscaler capex expectations are a meaningful demand tailwind, but those expectations are forecasts rather than realized spending and do not by themselves establish NVIDIA revenue.

limitations: FY2027 annual revenue and segment outcomes are not yet actual results; Q2 revenue is guidance and later-quarter estimates are forecasts.
Demand indicators, customer plans, and capex expectations do not translate one-for-one into NVIDIA recognized revenue.
watch_questions: Do subsequent reported quarters sustain the Q1 Data Center and Compute & Networking run rates?
Do customer infrastructure constraints, concentration, or China-market restrictions materially affect shipments or revenue?

heads.title: Vera Rubin has credible production-readiness signals, but delivery and deployment milestones remain forward-looking
heads.thesis: Current research supports the view that NVIDIA is preparing for Vera Rubin production shipments in the second half of 2026: management has given a schedule, and manufacturing and customer validation have advanced. The limitation is that the evidence does not establish that volume shipments have begun; downstream factory and satellite milestones are also plans, not completed deployments.

claims.text: Management has said Vera Rubin production shipments are expected in the second half of 2026, starting in Q3; this is direct schedule guidance, not confirmation that shipments have begun.
CoreWeave completed Vera Rubin NVL72 bring-up and validation, and Wistron is preparing a factory to produce Vera Rubin; these are readiness signals rather than proof of NVIDIA volume shipments.
Supply-chain delay risk remains contrary evidence to the stated schedule.
SK Telecom’s first AI factory is planned to come online in 2027 using DSX and Vera Rubin, but the broader SK–NVIDIA cooperation has not been shown to be formally finalized.
A 2027 launch of Starmind satellites using optimized Vera Rubin NVL72 is supported by a stated expectation and cooperation reports, but no launch is yet confirmed as having occurred.

limitations: The shipment and deployment conclusions are based largely on company or partner statements about future events.
Manufacturing preparation and system validation do not prove that production shipments or downstream deployments have occurred.
watch_questions: Is there confirmation of Vera Rubin production shipments beginning in the stated period?
Are the SK cooperation terms finalized, and does the first AI factory actually come online in 2027?
Does a Starmind satellite carrying the specified system launch by the stated deadline?

heads.title: High growth spending is guided alongside mid-70s gross margins, leaving operating leverage uncertain
heads.thesis: Current research supports a mixed operating profile for FY2027: management continues to guide to mid-70s full-year gross margins while expecting operating expenses to grow in the upper 40s. This indicates that strong gross-margin guidance does not, by itself, establish improving operating leverage; the annual outcomes remain unconfirmed.

claims.text: Management continues to expect full-year FY2027 gross margins in the mid-70s; Q1 non-GAAP gross margin was 75.0%, but that single-quarter actual does not determine the full year.
Management expects FY2027 operating expenses to grow in the upper 40s year over year, while Q1 non-GAAP operating expenses were up 49%; the full-year figure remains guidance, not an actual result.
Input-cost and margin-sustainability concerns provide contrary context, but the cited evidence does not establish that full-year gross margin will fall below management’s guidance.

limitations: Full-year gross margin and operating-expense growth are forward-looking expectations, not completed FY2027 results.
The non-GAAP operating-expense comparison may be affected by the company’s change in non-GAAP treatment of stock-based compensation.
watch_questions: Do subsequent quarters keep gross margins near the mid-70s, or do cost pressures alter the full-year outlook?
Does operating-expense growth moderate or remain near the guided upper-40s rate?

heads.title: Vera CPU offers a material new revenue opportunity, but the current evidence centers on guidance
heads.thesis: Current research supports a meaningful FY2027 Vera and standalone-CPU revenue opportunity, centered on management’s expectation of roughly $20 billion. Product announcements, customer interest, and planned shipments provide commercialization context, but they do not confirm realized revenue or support a higher annual amount on their own.

claims.text: Management’s expectation for standalone CPU revenue is close to $20 billion, which supports a middle-range FY2027 estimate rather than a higher amount; it is a forecast, not realized revenue.
NVIDIA’s Vera product sales expectation is also around $20 billion; performance claims and customer or partner announcements provide limited upside context but no higher revenue amount.
The expectation’s verifiability is a concern if standalone CPU revenue is not separately disclosed; competition from established server CPU suppliers is also a limitation on the commercial outlook.
The expected CPU-only rack shipment timing and Vera commercialization signals support launch prospects, but do not establish that shipments or revenue have already occurred.

limitations: The principal revenue anchor is management guidance, not reported FY2027 revenue.
Standalone CPU revenue and broader Vera product sales are related but should not be treated as identical measures.
watch_questions: Does NVIDIA disclose standalone CPU revenue separately in subsequent reporting?
Do Vera shipments begin on schedule, and do reported sales support the roughly $20 billion expectation?
